::: {.callout-tip}
## What we are building

A Stata project that rebuilds the levels curve of Jordà and Taylor's first
Monte Carlo example one regression at a time, reproduces the published
benchmark once the number of draws matches, and then carries the same moves from the
twelve rows of Lecture 01's hand table to a century of quarterly data on
military news. When it runs clean you can say what each point on a response
graph is: which regression produced it, from which rows, averaged over what,
and what it has not yet shown. The **[complete lab
project](p01-question-to-projection-lab.zip)** contains the starter do-files,
the solved problem set, the data with provenance, and automated checks. The **[instructor
build](build/index.qmd)** is the executed version.
:::

## The question

[Lecture 01](../../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd) asked how a
regression coefficient becomes one point on an impulse-response function, and
answered in an economy where the answer is known. If
$y_t=\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0 s_t+v_t$ with an observed shock $s_t$, the
regression of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$ has population
coefficient $\theta_0\rho^h$. A published local-projection result rests on the
same arithmetic, but the arithmetic sits inside someone else's do-file, behind
their variable names, their loop, and their choice of what to store. So the
practicum asks:

> **Can you rebuild a published local-projection result one regression at a
> time, and say exactly what each number in it measures?**

Part A answers the question for the smallest published target in the course
readings, the levels curve in Figure 1a of @jordataylor2025. Its economy is
the lecture's AR(1) with $\rho=0.95$ and $T=100$, so the true response is known
and every gap between the curve and the truth can be read. Part B repeats the
moves on the lecture's own anchors: the hand table, one simulated draw, a Monte
Carlo experiment, and the military-news data of @rameyzubairy2018. Part C
reruns in Stata what you predicted and computed in the browser.

## How to use the lab project

Download and unzip the **[lab project](p01-question-to-projection-lab.zip)**.
It unzips to a folder called `lab-project`. Set Stata's working folder to it
and run the master file:

```stata
cd "lab-project"
do master.do          // checks, REP01, your problem set, the handoff check
```

`master.do` runs four files in order and stops at the first check that fails:

1. `tests/checks.do` confirms, without a network connection, that the shipped
   data, benchmark, and vendor files have the SHA-256 values recorded in
   `data/PROVENANCE.md` and `vendor/jel-code/SOURCE.md`, that the simulated
   data follow their rules, that `data/raw/make_sim_data.do` regenerates them
   byte for byte, and that the helper programs in `helpers/lp_helpers.do`
   behave as documented;
2. `replication/rep01.do` rebuilds the REP01 target and compares it with three
   references;
3. `starter/pset.do` runs your problem set;
4. `handoff/check_handoff.do` reruns what the Shock-to-Response Explorer
   computed for you.

Everything lands in `output/`: `master.log` and one log per step,
`assertions.csv` with every check and its result, `rep01-benchmark.csv`, and
the two REP01 figures. The problem set writes its deliverables to
`output/pset/`. Two globals change the work. `global R` sets the number of
Monte Carlo draws, 200 by default (editor decision D2), and
`global AUTHOR_CHECK 0` skips the run of the authors' own script. With the
defaults, the checks and REP01 take about 30 seconds in StataNow/SE 19.5, and
a completed problem set about 30 seconds more, the download in Task 5 included;
the instructor build, with $R=500$, took 137 seconds from start
to `MASTER COMPLETE`. No user-written commands are needed.

While you work on the problem set, run `do starter/pset.do` on its own from
the same folder; keep the master file for the final record. The archive also
holds the solved problem set, `solution/pset_solution.do`, and
`do master.do solution` runs it in place of the starter. Open it after you have
attempted every task.

## Part A · Replication lab REP01

### The target

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Paper and version | @jordataylor2025, *Journal of Economic Literature* 63(1), 59–110. Replication package `ojorda/JEL-Code`, commit `655696c1c576b7537c5a939d2c261f0a111ae663` (CC0); the four files REP01 needs ship in `vendor/jel-code/`, with only the authors' two `cap cd` folder paths commented out |
| Exact target | Figure 1a, the levels curve: the Monte Carlo mean of $\hat\beta_h$ from ``reg f`h'.y vy l.y``, $h=0,\dots,10$, with an intercept and without the lagged difference, in an AR(1) with $\rho=0.95$ and $T=100$ after 500 burn-in periods, seed 12345 |
| Kind | Statistical reproduction. The published figure averages 10,000 draws; the instructor build averages 500 and the student default 200 (D2). At a matched draw count the reproduction is exact |
| Data and vintage | None external: the script simulates its data. Package frozen on 2026-09-13 |
| Original code | `Example1_LongDifferences/SSBias_IntcpYLagdiffN_95.do` (the authors' file, SHA-256 `07116508…4682a1e7e2`; `vendor/jel-code/SOURCE.md` records the shipped copy's): settings, lines 20–27; seed, line 39; simulated data, lines 45–63 (intervention `vy` on line 52, disturbance `e` on line 56, recursion on line 59, burn-in dropped on line 62); levels regressions, lines 84–90 (line 87); stored draws, lines 125–128; Monte Carlo means, lines 139–140; true response, lines 156–168. Driver `all-simulate.do`, lines 18–19 (`nobs 100`, `nreps 10000`) |
| Benchmark | The course benchmark `REP01-levels-lp.csv`: the authors' script at 500 draws in Stata/SE 18.5, from 1.00175750 at $h=0$ to 0.43152007 at $h=10$. Two further references: the same script at 200 draws in StataNow/SE 19.5 (0.99686521 to 0.42771590) and the authors' shipped 10,000-draw means (0.99697095 to 0.42890212). The instructor build reproduces the 500-draw benchmark with a largest absolute difference of $4\times10^{-8}$ |
| Tolerance | Absolute $10^{-6}$ on every mean when the draw counts match. Against the 10,000-draw means, $\lvert z\rvert<3$, where $z$ is the difference divided by $\mathrm{sd}_R\sqrt{1/R+1/10{,}000}$ |
| Deliberate departures | Draws reduced from 10,000 (D2). The course code leaves out the authors' `$a*l.d.y` term, which is zero in this variant (line 57 sets `a` to 0.00), stores each draw as `double` where the authors store `float`, and records $T_h$ from `e(N)`, which the authors do not keep. The long-difference, cumulative-difference, and AR(1) curves of the same figure belong to REP02. The authors' `cap cd` lines, commented out in the shipped copy so that the archive holds no absolute path, and their Palatino font setting have no effect in batch |
| Runtime | Instructor build ($R=500$): Monte Carlo 15.1 s, authors' script 46.4 s, the whole REP01 file 63.7 s. Student default ($R=200$): 26.6 s for the REP01 file, 18.6 s of it in the authors' script |

### Reconstruct the specification

`replication/rep01.do` rebuilds the target in five steps, and a sixth step is
yours. The blocks below follow that file. To run them yourself, start Stata in
the project's top folder, type `do helpers/lp_helpers.do`, which loads
`lp_assert` and `lp_close`, and then run the blocks of Steps 2 to 5 in order in
the same session.

#### Step 1 · Read the authors' simulation

The whole target comes from about twenty lines of the authors' script. Read
them before running anything.

```stata
* SSBias_IntcpYLagdiffN_95.do, lines 39-62 (blank lines removed, indentation normalized)
set seed 12345
qui forvalues i = 1(1)$nreps{
    noi disp "`i'," , _continue
    preserve
    clear
    set obs  $tobs
    gen t = _n
    sort t, stable
    tsset t
    *** Generate data from the model
    gen vy  = rnormal()
    gen y   = 0
        *!!! add noise and lagdiff
        gen e=rnormal()
        global a 0.00
    replace y = $rho * l.y + $a * l.d.y + vy + e    if _n > 2
    *** Drop the burn-in sample
    drop if _n <= $burn

* lines 83-90
    *** Estimate the LP in levels
    forvalues h = 0/$hmax{
*       reg f`h'.y y
*       local b_level_`h' = _b[y]
        reg f`h'.y vy l.y /*l.d.y*/  // cons and N lag diff
        local b_level_`h' = _b[vy]
        }
```

**Read the result.** In the lecture's notation `vy` is the intervention $s_t$
and `e` the disturbance $v_t$; both are standard normal, and all 600 values of
`vy` are drawn before any value of `e`. Line 59 is
$y_t=0.95\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t$, so $\theta_0=1$ and the true response is
$\theta_h=0.95^h$, which lines 156–168 store as `rt`. The first two periods
stay at zero, and the 500 periods dropped on line 62 make that start
irrelevant. Line 87 is the
[local projection of the lecture's smallest model](../../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-lp-toy)
with $\mathbf w_t=y_{t-1}$ and $p=1$. After the burn-in the sample has $T=100$
periods; `l.y` is missing in the first of them and `f`h'.y` in the last $h$,
so the regression at horizon $h$ uses $T_h=99-h$ rows. The authors keep the
coefficient and nothing else: no row count and no standard error.

**Checkpoint.** Before `restore`, the loop also fits an AR(1), long
differences, and cumulated differences. Say why none of those regressions can
change the draws that the levels regression sees.

#### Step 2 · One realization, one horizon

Rebuild the first draw outside the loop and run the $h=0$ regression.

```stata
local rho  = 0.95
local burn = 500
local tobs = 600
clear
set seed 12345
set obs `tobs'
generate t = _n
tsset t
generate vy = rnormal()           // line 52: the intervention s_t, drawn first
generate y  = 0                   // line 53: stored as float, as in the authors' code
generate e  = rnormal()           // line 56: the disturbance v_t, drawn second
replace y = `rho'*L.y + vy + e if _n > 2      // line 59; the term in a is zero
drop if _n <= `burn'              // line 62: keep the last 100 periods
replace t = _n
tsset t
regress F0.y vy L.y
lp_assert "REP01 step 1: the h = 0 regression has T_0 = 99 rows" : e(N) == 99
lp_close _b[vy] 1.06035137, tol(1e-6) label(REP01 step 1: draw 1 at h = 0)
```

**Read the result.** The first draw gives $\hat\beta_0=1.060351$ on 99 rows,
0.06 above $\theta_0=1$. The block keeps the authors' storage of `y` as a
`float`, so this is their first draw, not a draw like it. The check's target,
1.06035137, is the coefficient as the authors' `float` variable holds it:
`display %11.8f float(_b[vy])` prints it after the regression. The build's
`double` copy, 1.06035143, differs from it by $6\times10^{-8}$.

**Checkpoint.** Both checks pass. Explain the 99 without running anything:
which row is lost, and why.

#### Step 3 · The same draw at every horizon

```stata
tempfile draw1
tempname D
postfile `D' h double b_draw1 T_draw1 using `draw1'
forvalues h = 0/10 {
    quietly regress F`h'.y vy L.y
    post `D' (`h') (_b[vy]) (e(N))
}
postclose `D'
use `draw1', clear
list, clean noobs
lp_assert "REP01 step 2: T_h = 99 - h in draw 1" : T_draw1 == 99 - h
```

**Read the result.** Rounded to six decimals, draw 1 gives 1.060351, 0.999817,
0.596461, 0.555731, 0.403161, 0.213559, 0.088265, −0.148038, −0.282293,
−0.250712, and 0.243100 at $h=0,\dots,10$. The true response never falls below
$0.95^{10}=0.599$. This sample says the response turns negative seven periods
out and recovers by the tenth, and neither statement is true of the economy
that produced it. Posting `e(N)` with the coefficient keeps each point attached
to its rows, and `rep01.do` checks all eleven values against the authors'
stored ones at $10^{-6}$.

**Checkpoint.** In the second figure of the instructor build, find the
horizons at which draw 1 lies outside the middle 90 percent of the 500 draws.
Use [the lecture's section on the residual](../../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-residual)
to explain why those horizons sit next to each other.

#### Step 4 · The Monte Carlo

```stata
capture mkdir output
if "$R" == "" global R 200            // the student default (D2); master.do sets it
tempname M
postfile `M' rep h double b T_h using "output/rep01-draws.dta", replace
set seed 12345                        // once, before the loop, as on line 39
quietly forvalues r = 1/$R {
    clear
    set obs 600
    generate t = _n
    tsset t
    generate vy = rnormal()
    generate y  = 0
    generate e  = rnormal()
    replace y = 0.95*L.y + vy + e if _n > 2
    drop if _n <= 500
    replace t = _n
    tsset t
    forvalues h = 0/10 {
        regress F`h'.y vy L.y
        post `M' (`r') (`h') (_b[vy]) (e(N))
    }
}
postclose `M'
use "output/rep01-draws.dta", clear
lp_assert "REP01: every draw has T_h = 99 - h rows" : T_h == 99 - h
collapse (mean) mean_R=b (sd) sd_R=b, by(h)
```

**Read the result.** With $R=500$ the instructor build reproduces the
benchmark at every horizon. Six of the eleven rows, rounded as shown:

| $h$ | $\theta_h$ | Benchmark, 500 draws, Stata 18.5 | This build, 500 draws, StataNow 19.5 | Monte Carlo SE |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1.0000 | 1.00175750 | 1.00175746 | 0.0047 |
| 2 | 0.9025 | 0.86787397 | 0.86787396 | 0.0103 |
| 4 | 0.8145 | 0.73754936 | 0.73754938 | 0.0135 |
| 6 | 0.7351 | 0.62550861 | 0.62550860 | 0.0159 |
| 8 | 0.6634 | 0.51882571 | 0.51882570 | 0.0177 |
| 10 | 0.5987 | 0.43152007 | 0.43152008 | 0.0178 |

The benchmark column is the file as
`import delimited using "replication/benchmark/REP01-levels-lp.csv", clear varnames(1) encoding(utf8)`
reads it, the line `rep01.do` runs before it compares; `asdouble` returns the
same eight decimals. The two columns never differ by as much as
$5\times10^{-8}$, and what difference there is comes from storage: the authors
average `float` draws and the course averages `double` draws. The mean lies
below $\theta_h$ at every horizon from $h=1$ on, by 0.025 at $h=1$ and by
0.167 at $h=10$, which is 9.4 Monte Carlo standard errors. That gap belongs to
the estimator in samples of 100 periods with $\rho=0.95$, not to the
reproduction; Lecture 2 explains it.

**Checkpoint.** At the default $R=200$ your means must equal the authors' own
200-draw run, `replication/benchmark/REP01-author-R200-v195.csv`, at
$10^{-6}$, and `rep01.do` also checks them against the 500-draw benchmark
within three nested Monte Carlo standard errors. If every draw returns the
same estimate, `set seed` has moved inside the loop.

#### Step 5 · Two cross-checks

The first runs the authors' script itself at the same number of
draws; the second compares the build with the 10,000 draws of the published
figure.

```stata
tempfile summary author10000
save `summary'                        // the means and standard deviations of Step 4

* the authors' script at the same R, from a folder of its own
local here = c(pwd)
capture mkdir "output/rep01-author"
quietly cd "output/rep01-author"
global nobs = 100
global nreps = $R
quietly do "`here'/vendor/jel-code/SSBias_IntcpYLagdiffN_95.do"
quietly cd "`here'"
keep t rl                             // rl: the authors' mean of the levels estimates
rename (t rl) (h author_R)
merge 1:1 h using `summary', nogenerate assert(match)
lp_assert "REP01 cross-check: the authors' script and Step 4 agree at every h (1e-6)" : abs(author_R - mean_R) < 1e-6

* the published figure's means, treated as an independent stream of 10,000 draws
preserve
use "vendor/jel-code/SSBias_IntcpYLagdiffN_95.dta", clear
keep t rl
rename (t rl) (h author_10000)
save `author10000'
restore
merge 1:1 h using `author10000', nogenerate assert(match)
generate double se_10000 = sd_R*sqrt(1/$R + 1/10000)
generate double z_10000  = (mean_R - author_10000)/se_10000
format mean_R author_R author_10000 %11.8f
format z_10000 %6.2f
list h mean_R author_R author_10000 z_10000, clean noobs
lp_assert "REP01 statistical: |z| < 3 against the 10,000-draw means at every h" : abs(z_10000) < 3
```

**Read the result.** At $R=500$ the authors' script and `rep01.do` agree at
every horizon within $4\times10^{-8}$. The authors' shipped 10,000-draw means
differ from the 500-draw means by at most 0.018, at $h=2$, where $z=1.71$, and
no horizon comes near $\lvert z\rvert=3$. The published figure is reproduced
as a statistical object; the 500-draw curve is the authors' own curve at that
draw count.

**Checkpoint.** Explain why the comparison with the 10,000-draw means cannot
be exact, and why its standard error adds $1/10{,}000$ to $1/R$ rather than
subtracting it.

#### Step 6 · Write the construction note

In about 150 words, write down what REP01 reproduces for a reader who has only
Figure 1a: which variable is $s_t$ and how it is drawn, which rows enter the
regression at horizon $h$ and how many, what the curve averages and over how
many draws, and what the authors' output does not contain. Add one sentence on
the gap between the curve and $0.95^h$ that describes it without explaining it.

**Checkpoint.** Someone else should be able to rerun the target from your note
and `vendor/jel-code/` alone.

### Discrepancy guidance

When your number differs, record it before you change anything. A row of the
discrepancy log has six fields: the **object** (which mean, at which horizon,
at which $R$), the **published** value and its source, the **reproduced**
value, the **class** (data, specification, software, inference, or
presentation), a **diagnosis**, and a **status** (resolved, accepted as a
departure, or open). For this target the likely causes are few, and each
leaves a recognizable trace.

| What you see | Most likely cause | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Every mean within $10^{-7}$ of the reference but not identical to it | `float` versus `double` storage of the draws or of `y` | software |
| Every mean off by more than $10^{-6}$ but by less than three Monte Carlo standard errors | a different random stream: `e` drawn before `vy`, another seed, or another `set obs` | specification |
| A standard deviation of zero across draws | `set seed` inside the loop | specification |
| $T_h=599-h$ | the burn-in was never dropped | specification |
| $T_h=100-h$ | `L.y` left out of the regression, which also changes the estimate | specification |
| Your means match the 200-draw file but not the 500-draw benchmark | a different $R$: compare with the reference for your draw count | specification |
| A curve with a different shape or level everywhere | another variant of the script: `IntcpN` drops the intercept, `LagdiffY` adds $\Delta y_{t-1}$ (REP02) | specification |
| A difference between Stata 18.5 and StataNow 19.5 beyond $10^{-6}$ | a software change (D1); the instructor build found none | software |

## Part B · Stata problem set STA01

The problem set runs the lecture's argument in the order construct, estimate,
diagnose, interpret. `starter/pset.do` gives the data steps, the files to
write, and the checks; the lines marked `TASK` are yours. The checks are the
`lp_assert` and `lp_close` lines at the end of each task. Each prints `pass` or
`FAIL`, and the first failure stops the file. They test what a machine can
test; the captions in Tasks 4 and 5 and the paragraph in Task 5 are read by a
person against the slots and sentences listed below. The tasks follow
Exercises 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 of the
[Lecture 01 exercises](../../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-exercises),
whose hints apply here. A worked answer ships as `solution/pset_solution.do`,
and the [instructor build](build/index.qmd) shows it task by task with its
output; read either after your own attempt.

### Task 1 · Construct the rows for $h=0,1,2$

Read the hand table (`data/raw/hand_table.csv`, or the copy that the
Explorer's Lab 2 exports) and, for each horizon, mark the rows of the
regression of $y_{t+h}$ on $s_t$ and $y_{t-1}$ without running it: the lead
$y_{t+h}$, the rows with $t\ge2$ and a lead that exists, and their counts.

- **Deliverable.** `output/pset/results_hand.dta` with `h`, `T_h`, `n1`
  (intervention rows), `n0` (comparison rows), `first`, and `last`.
- **Checks.** $T_h=11-h$; every row is an intervention row or a comparison row;
  the rows run from $t=2$ to $t=12-h$; three intervention rows at $h=0$ and two
  at $h=1$ and $h=2$.

### Task 2 · Estimate the slopes from the rows

On the same rows, compute the group means $\bar y_1$ and $\bar y_0$, compute
the slope by hand as $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)\,y_{t+h}/\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$,
confirm it with `regress`, and add $y_{t-1}$ on the same rows.

- **Deliverable.** The means and the three slopes, added to `results_hand.dta`.
- **Checks.** The slope by hand equals $\bar y_1-\bar y_0$ within $10^{-6}$;
  `regress` returns the same slope; both regressions use exactly the rows of
  Task 1; the slopes are 0.617322, −0.983356, and 2.050024 without the control
  and 0.575667, −1.050405, and 2.153022 with it.

### Task 3 · A response in a loop

On `onedraw_rho09_seed2.csv`, the $T=200$ sample that Lab 3 displays, regress
$y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$ for $h=0,\dots,12$, posting each
coefficient with its `e(N)`.

- **Deliverable.** `output/pset/results_onedraw.dta` with `h`, `beta_h`, and
  `T_h`.
- **Checks.** $T=200$; $T_h=199-h$; $\hat\beta_0=0.878940$ and
  $\hat\beta_{12}=-0.293297$ within $10^{-6}$; the estimate lies below
  $\theta_h=0.9^h$ at all thirteen horizons.

### Task 4 · Many draws, one graph, a caption with four slots

Write the Monte Carlo loop of Exercise 7: seed 3 set once for each
$\rho\in\{0.5,0.9\}$, 300 periods with all of $s$ drawn before any $v$, the
first 100 dropped, and at each horizon the slope with and without $y_{t-1}$.
The given code summarizes the first 200 samples. Then draw Task 3's estimates
against $0.9^h$ with the simulated 5–95 percent band. Fill the caption's four
slots before you draw: what one unit of the intervention is, the outcome's
units, the horizon unit, and what a value of zero is compared with.

- **Deliverable.** `output/pset/mc_draws.dta`, `mc_R200_summary.dta`,
  `fig-sta01-one-draw.svg` and `.png`, and `fig-sta01-one-draw-caption.txt`.
- **Checks.** $199-h$ rows with the control and $200-h$ without; with $R=200$,
  at $\rho=0.9$ and $h=8$, a mean of 0.370337 and a standard deviation of
  0.211226 within $10^{-6}$; without the control a larger spread at every
  horizon when $\rho=0.9$; all four caption slots filled; the graph exported.
  The caption is read for the four slots.

### Task 5 · Military news: the response, its variation, one episode

`data/raw/get_rz.do` downloads Ramey and Zubairy's February 2018 package from
the authors' link and verifies its SHA-256, or prints the manual steps; the
course does not redistribute the workbook (D5, D35). The starter reads it with
`import excel using "data/raw/RZDAT.xlsx", sheet("rzdat") firstrow clear`.
Trend GDP is Ramey and Zubairy's `rgdp_pott6`, the series they call potential
GDP and estimate as a sixth-degree polynomial trend in real GDP. Build
$y_t=\texttt{rgdp}_t/\texttt{rgdp\_pott6}_t$ and the news as a fraction of the
previous quarter's nominal trend GDP, estimate the response for
$h=0,\dots,20$, compute each quarter's share of $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$ in the
$h=8$ sample, re-estimate $h=8$ without 1950Q3, and write the caption and a
five-sentence paragraph headed "What has not yet been argued."

- **Deliverable.** `output/pset/first_contact.dta`, `sta01-news-shares.csv`,
  `fig-sta01-first-contact.svg` and `.png`, the caption file, and
  `not-yet-argued.txt`.
- **Checks.** 508 consecutive quarters; the news recorded in 504 of them; the
  news in 1950Q3 equal to 0.600073; $T_h=504-h$; $\hat\beta_8=0.361906$ and
  $\hat\beta_{10}=0.404210$, with the peak at $h=10$; 1941Q4 and 1950Q3 the two
  largest shares, 0.261211 and 0.195838; without 1950Q3, 0.433969 on 495 rows;
  with Ramey and Zubairy's controls, 0.29376385 at $h=10$ on 490 rows, the
  linear GDP response in the course's REP04 benchmark. The paragraph is read
  for one sentence each on units, controls, identification, uncertainty, and
  dependence on a few episodes.

## Part C · The browser-lab handoff

The "Transfer to Stata" section of the
[Shock-to-Response Explorer](../../interactives/01-shock-to-response-explorer.qmd)
writes three files: `l01-explorer-handoff.json`, `hand_table.csv`, and the draw
file chosen in Lab 3. Put them in the project's `handoff/` folder, replacing
the sample there; `handoff/README.md` in the archive lists every key of the
record.

| Explorer lab | What the record holds | Where Stata uses it |
|---|---|---|
| Lab 2 | `hand_table.csv`; the chosen $h$, control, and single-episode setting; the browser's $T_h$ and slope | Tasks 1–2 read the file when its SHA-256 equals the shipped copy's; `check_handoff.do` reruns the regression |
| Lab 3 | The draw file, $T$, the control choice, and thirteen slopes and row counts | Task 3 reads the draw when its values equal the shipped copy's; `check_handoff.do` reruns all thirteen regressions |
| Lab 4 | Your hypothesis about the $h=8$ coefficient without 1950Q3, and the stored estimate for your settings | Task 5 prints the hypothesis beside its own estimate; `check_handoff.do` re-estimates the stored coefficient and sets the hypothesis against it |

Lab 4 displays only estimates computed in Stata from the Ramey–Zubairy data,
never data rows (D33), so its part of the check waits until Task 5 has
downloaded the workbook. The hypothesis is read for a direction (raise, lower,
or unchanged) and a number, and the verdict goes to
`output/handoff-check.csv` without a grade. The sample record shipped with the
project predicts that dropping 1950Q3 lowers the estimate to about 0.30. The
estimate rises, from 0.361906 to 0.433969, and the check records the
prediction as refuted.

## Submission package

| Deliverable | Required contents |
|---|---|
| Replication record | The target (Figure 1a, levels curve, $h=0,\dots,10$), the package commit, the draw count you ran, `output/rep01-benchmark.csv`, a sentence comparing your StataNow run with the Stata 18.5 benchmark at your draw count, the construction note of Step 6, and any discrepancy-log rows |
| Stata submission | The project folder with your `starter/pset.do`; `output/master.log` ending in `MASTER COMPLETE`; `output/assertions.csv`; the `output/pset/` files listed under each task; the REP01 figures |
| Interpretation record | For Task 5: the estimand $\theta_h$ and the assumptions under which $\beta_h=\theta_h$, the units of the news and of GDP relative to trend, the absence of standard errors, and the "not yet argued" paragraph |
| Lab record | Your `l01-explorer-handoff.json` with its four predictions, `output/handoff-check.csv`, and one paragraph on what the chain of four labs showed you |

## Mastery requirement

The practicum is done when you can say, with the numbers from your own run and
without notes:

> Each point of the levels curve is the coefficient on $s_t$ in a regression of
> $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$ over $99-h$ rows, averaged
> over the draws; at 500 draws it reproduces the published benchmark to within
> $10^{-6}$, and it lies below $0.95^h$ for a reason Lecture 2 explains. In the
> military-news data the same regression averages over every quarter with news,
> weighted by $(s_t-\bar s)^2$, so two war quarters carry 46 percent of its
> variation and dropping one of them moves the estimate at $h=8$ by 0.07. It is
> not yet the causal response to the news: its units, controls,
> identification, and uncertainty are still to be argued.
